facts.text: Director Buddy Giovinazzo borrowed lights and camera gear from the film school where he taught, and even put money from his own wedding into the movie.
The budget is listed at about $40,000. Cast and crew worked unpaid; money mostly went to food and lab costs.
Before Troma bought it, the film played festivals under the title "American Nightmares."
Staten Island was the whole set: shot without permits or permission on real streets, mostly in Port Richmond, where Giovinazzo grew up.
The deformed baby puppet cost just $140 to make. Its voice is Buddy's own, sped up and played backwards.
The Vietnam jungle was the swamps of Staten Island. The torture hut was built in the director's mother's backyard.
Frankie's army uniform and the rest of the wardrobe came from a local Salvation Army.
Buddy shot sync-sound apartment scenes on a CP-16 and silent jungle, effects and chase scenes on a Bolex. He said the Bolex was "like a tank."
The film's synth score was composed by Rick Giovinazzo, who also plays Frankie. He later became an orchestrator on Hollywood blockbusters like Transformers.
Other actors screen-tested for Frankie before Buddy cast his brother Rick, who was in grad school at the time.
Buddy cast friends, family and film school students in small roles. Comedian Eddie Pepitone plays a strung-out junkie.
The brothers, trained as studio musicians, built oppressive industrial-factory sound design inspired by David Lynch and Alan Splet's work on Eraserhead.
The effects team tried aging the rented house with latex and ink. The ink bled into the walls and the whole house had to be repainted.
Fake blood from a bedroom scene seeped through the floorboards of the rented house and alarmed the landlord at a later showing.
Some jungle scenes were shot with only the director, his brother Rick and one crew member. There was no production designer or line producer.
Shooting had no schedule pressure. Some days ran five hours, others fourteen.
Troma sold the film as a Rambo-style action flick, which misled audiences about what it was.
Troma trimmed about 8 minutes from the 100-minute "American Nightmares" cut. Buddy says he never sanctioned the trims on the Troma DVD.
The R-rated version of the film is heavily cut. The unrated Troma VHS from the late 1990s is the only way to see the uncut Troma theatrical edit.
Lloyd Kaufman insisted in 2004 that no footage was missing from the Troma edit. Buddy, in an interview that January, said otherwise.
The TMDB tagline: "Fighting, killing, maiming. Agent Orange and the torture cages were the easy part!"
Vincent Canby of The New York Times called it a "family affair" that "means to be shocking but it more often prompts giggles."
facts.byline: Vincent Canby — The New York Times

facts.text: Buddy said, "Combat Shock really hurt me. It wasn't liked by anybody for years." He turned to writing novels, including Life Is Hot in Cracktown.
Buddy later made the short Mr. Robbie (1989) with Joe Spinell and tried to expand it into a feature before Spinell died.
Critics compared it to Eraserhead and Taxi Driver. Film Threat called it an antithesis to Platoon and Apocalypse Now.
The film is a time capsule of 1980s Staten Island because it was shot on real streets and train stations, not in a studio. Many locations remain unchanged 25 years later.
Toxie gets a nod: The Toxic Avenger Part III references Combat Shock. So does the 2009 documentary Post Traumatic: An American Nightmare.
The Troma 2009 two-disc DVD includes both the Troma cut and the original American Nightmares cut, plus a commentary with Nekromantik director Jorg Buttgereit.
Directors like Richard Stanley, Jim VanBebber and William Lustig discuss the film's impact in the documentary "Post-Traumatic: An American Nightmare."
Buddy Giovinazzo graduated with a Masters in Cinema from the College of Staten Island. He later taught at NYU and the School of Visual Arts.
Veronica Stork, who plays Cathy, later turned up in Class of Nuke 'Em High Part II: Subhumanoid Meltdown (1991).
Severin Films released a limited edition with new commentaries, early shorts, the soundtrack and a 96-page book of Buddy's shoot diary.
DVD Talk called it "so bleak it's almost laughable, but the pathos is too real, even with a mutant baby."
Combat Shock has since moved from reviled to cult: Troma released a 2022 Blu-ray with a new Lloyd Kaufman intro.
